newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Veteran newsman returns to Kwangju massacre site.
newsitem.headline: Veteran newsman returns to Kwangju massacre site.

text.p: Armed with small movie camera, and spools of film that he smuggled past military checkpoints inside his shirt, German television reporter Jurgen Hinzpeter shocked the world with graphic images of the 1980 Kwangju massacre.
On Sunday, he returned to the South Korean city to cover the first officially sponsored anniversary mourning rites for the more than 200 victims of the army slaughter.

Combat-trained troops stormed Kwangju to crush an armed revolt against martial law imposed by then-general Chun Doo Hwan, who later became president. Residents say the true death toll may have been several thousand, killed by machine-gun fire, rifle butts and bayonets.

Hinzpeter, 59, a veteran newsman who had covered the Vietnam War, was completely unprepared for the carnage that greeted him when he arrived in Kwangju two days after the paratroopers had gone on the rampage.
At that point, the full horror of the tragedy had not leaked out. All telephone lines to Kwangju were cut.
"I was shocked to see rows of coffins with young students," he said. "I had to film with constant tears blurring my vision."
"People were in grief everywhere and I was overwhelmed by the anger of the citizens."
He added: "I covered the Vietnam War, but I had never experienced anything like Kwangju".
The worst of the killing took place on May 18. Hinzpeter, then with the German television company Norddeutscher Rundfunk, talked his way past nervous soldiers to reach the city on May 20.

His film of bodies being loaded onto open trucks, of terrified citizens being led away by troops at gunpoint and of fires sputtering in buildings were some of the most dramatic documentary evidence of the tragedy.
To get the film back to Seoul on a commercial flight, Hinzpeter wrapped the metal boxes in silver foil and tied the heavy bundle in ribbons to make it look like a wedding gift.

For years, grainy copies of the colour film circulated underground in South Korea, passed secretly among student and Christian groups. The Seoul government for a long time denied any killings occurred, and censored publications that claimed otherwise. Hinzpeter's film exposed the lie.
In the West, the footage was syndicated around Europe and the United States.

"Most of the students were killing in shootings, but many that I saw in coffins had major blows to their heads. They must have been beaten to death," said Hinzpeter, now a freelancer based in Hamburg.
He said he spent sleepless nights in Kwangju listening to the gunfire, screaming citizens and mothers crying over their dead sons and daughters.

Hinzpeter was joined at Sunday's ceremonies by several other foreign correspondents who covered the massacre, among them Norman Thorpe, then of the Asian Wall Street Journal, and Sam Jameson of the Los Angeles Times.
Terry Anderson, the former Associated Press reporter later kidnapped in Lebanon, originally intended to return but in the end did not make it, Hinzpeter said.
"I hope Kwangju served a lesson for everyone on democracy. Hopefully, it will not happen again," he said.
